title: The Night the Stars Asked Questions

pages.text: The lights went out just after supper. "Oh, ECG!" exclaimed twelve-year-old Araba. Grandma Esi carried two chairs into the courtyard. "Come outside. The sky has something to show you." Araba looked up. Thousands of stars glittered above the village. "Grandma, how many stars are there?" "Far more than we can count by looking up tonight." "Does every star have planets?" "Not every star is known to have planets, but scientists have discovered thousands of planets around other stars." Araba leaned back. "Then there may be worlds we have never seen." Grandma smiled. "And questions we have not yet answered."

"And questions we have not yet answered."

pages.text: The following day, Araba told her science teacher about the stars. "Some stars are so far away that their light takes years to reach Earth," he explained. "Does that mean we see them as they were in the past?" "Yes. Looking into distant space is also looking back in time." Araba stared at the classroom window. "So a telescope can help us study history?" "The history of the universe," her teacher replied.

pages.text: During astronomy club, the teacher showed a diagram of a galaxy. "Scientists observe that visible matter alone does not explain all the gravitational effects they measure in galaxies and other cosmic structures." "What is missing?" Araba asked. "Scientists use the name dark matter for a proposed form of matter that helps explain those observations." "Have they caught some in a bottle?" The class laughed. "No confirmed direct detection of a dark-matter particle has yet established its nature. Researchers continue testing ideas." Araba wrote: Evidence can reveal a mystery without solving every part of it.

pages.text: Araba imagined a planet with two suns. "Wouldn't that be wonderful?" Her teacher explained that planets can orbit systems containing more than one star. "Some planets orbit two stars," he said. "But their conditions vary." "Could people live there?" "We do not know of such a planet where humans could live. We must distinguish an exciting possibility from evidence." Araba nodded. "Science is not simply guessing what would be nice." "Exactly. It is asking questions and testing explanations."

pages.text: One afternoon, Araba read a headline: ALIENS HAVE SENT A MESSAGE TO EARTH! She rushed to school. "Sir! Is this true?" Her teacher asked her to examine the source. The article provided no credible scientific evidence. "Some unusual signals have been investigated," he explained, "but that does not mean they were messages from extraterrestrial beings." Araba sighed. "I wanted it to be true." "Curiosity is wonderful," he replied. "But curiosity also requires patience and honesty."

pages.text: At home, Araba asked Grandma Esi, "Do you think life exists somewhere else in the universe?" Grandma considered the question. "I do not know. What does your teacher say?" "He says scientists are searching for evidence, but life beyond Earth has not been confirmed." Grandma nodded. "Then it is a question worth exploring." Araba smiled. "Sometimes the most interesting answer is, 'We do not know yet.'"

pages.text: Araba organized a small astronomy evening at school. The children used a star chart and, with adult supervision, a telescope to observe the night sky. They learned to identify some visible celestial objects and record their observations. One student asked whether the universe would keep expanding forever. Their teacher explained that cosmologists study the universe's expansion and its possible long-term future. "Scientists have strong evidence for cosmic expansion," he said, "but important questions remain about dark energy and the universe's ultimate fate."

pages.text: That night, Araba returned to the courtyard. Grandma Esi sat beside her. "Did you find the answer to every question?" Grandma asked. "No. I found more questions." "Are you disappointed?" Araba shook her head. "Not anymore. I want to become a scientist." "What will you discover?" Araba looked toward the stars. "I don't know yet." Then she grinned. "That is the exciting part."

activities.question: Why do scientists investigate dark matter?
options: Visible matter alone does not explain all observed gravity effects.
They have already caught bottles of dark matter in school labs.
Galaxies have no gravity at all.
activities.explanation: Observations of gravity and cosmic structures cannot be fully explained by visible matter alone within the standard cosmological framework.

activities.question: Why does distant starlight show us the past?
options: Light takes time to travel across space.
Stars only shine backwards in time.
Telescopes invent pictures of the past.
activities.explanation: Because light takes time to travel across vast distances, we see distant stars as they were when the light left them.

activities.question: Is life beyond Earth confirmed by science?
options: No; scientists are searching, but it has not been confirmed.
Yes; aliens have sent confirmed messages to every newspaper.
Yes; humans already live on a planet with two suns.
activities.explanation: No. Scientists are searching for evidence, but life beyond Earth has not been confirmed.

activities.question: What is dark matter?
options: A proposed form of matter inferred from gravitational observations
Ordinary black clouds of smoke from power stations
A fully understood particle kept in classroom bottles
activities.explanation: Dark matter is a proposed form of matter inferred from gravitational observations; its exact nature remains unknown.

activities.question: Should we believe an extraordinary headline without evidence?
options: No; check credible sources and supporting scientific evidence.
Yes; every exciting headline on the internet is true.
Yes; checking sources is a waste of time.
activities.explanation: No. We should examine the source and check for credible scientific evidence before believing extraordinary claims.

activities.prompt: Which of these is a genuine scientific question about the universe that researchers are still investigating?
options: What is the exact nature of dark matter and dark energy?
Does light travel instantaneously in zero seconds?
Are there only ten stars in the entire universe?

glossary.definition: An optical instrument that gathers light to make distant objects in space appear closer and clearer.
A vast system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
Relating to gravity, the force of attraction between masses in the universe.
The curved path of a planet, moon or spacecraft around a star or another celestial body.
Originating or existing outside Earth and its atmosphere.
Positioned in or relating to the sky or outer space, such as stars and planets.
Scientists who study the origin, structure, expansion and evolution of the universe.
